title: Inequalities
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 6; not yet checked by a Kenyan maths teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Inequalities are taught on a number line first (a filled dot when the boundary is allowed, an open dot when it is not), with the words "at least", "at most", "more than" and "fewer than" matched to the symbols. Simplifying uses the balance idea of Grade 5 equations, with the symbol kept the same way.

skills.key_step: The child decides whether the boundary number is allowed and which side is allowed, and then chooses the symbol.

floor.prerequisite: Uses < and > to compare two numbers.
floor.question: Put < or > : 12 __ 30

representations: the story acted with counters (some numbers allowed, some not)
a number line with an open or filled dot and a shaded side
steps: Find the boundary number in the story.
Ask: is the boundary itself allowed?
Ask: are bigger or smaller numbers allowed?
Write x with the symbol: >, <, >= or <=.
contexts: learners needed for a football team
shillings to spend at the canteen

board.do: Draw a number line from 10 to 18 with a dot at 14.
Write "A matatu carries at most 14 passengers."
Wait for yes, then fill the dot.
Ask the child to shade the side that is allowed.

misconceptions.ask: Fewer than 12: are 5 mandazi allowed? Are 20?
misconceptions.repair: The open end of the symbol faces the bigger number: x < 12.
At most 14 is a top limit: 14 or fewer.
A limit allows more than one number, so use an inequality.

checks.question: "Not more than 40 learners" as an inequality

skills.key_step: The child undoes the operation on the x side by doing its inverse to both sides and writes the same symbol on every line.
representations: a balance that tips to one side
the inequality with the same step written on both sides
a check with a number that should work
steps: Find what is done to x.
Do the inverse to both sides.
Check with a number from the answer.
contexts: money left after buying a book

board.do: Draw a balance tipped to the right with x + 5 on the left and 12 on the right.

board.say: What can we take off both sides?

board.do: Wait for the child to say 5.
Ask the child to write the answer and say whether the symbol changes.

misconceptions.ask: Does taking 4 from both sides change which side is lighter?
misconceptions.repair: Adding, subtracting or dividing by a positive number keeps the symbol the same.
Do the inverse: subtract 5 from both sides.

misconceptions.ask: What did you do to the 18?
misconceptions.repair: Both sides get the same step: 18 / 3 = 6.

skills.key_step: The child simplifies to x and a symbol, then lists or picks the whole numbers allowed, saying whether the boundary is one of them.
representations: a number line with the boundary dot and the allowed whole numbers circled
the two-step working, one line per step
a check by putting a number back in
steps: Undo adding or subtracting first, then multiplying or dividing.
Mark the boundary: open dot if not allowed, filled if allowed.
List or pick the whole numbers asked for and check one.
contexts: how many packets a learner can buy
learners that fit in a classroom
days left to save for a trip

board.do: Wait for the child to take 3 from both sides.
Draw a number line with an open dot at 7.
Ask the child to circle the largest whole number allowed.

misconceptions.repair: A strict symbol leaves the boundary out: the largest is 7.
An inequality has many answers; check each one.

misconceptions.ask: Is 3 more than 3? Is 8 less than 8?
misconceptions.repair: Leave out an end that is not allowed, then count.
The line under the symbol means the boundary is allowed.

misconceptions.ask: Put 7 into 2x + 4: is it less than 20?
misconceptions.repair: Take 4 from both sides first, then divide both sides by 2.

checks.question: What is the largest whole number with 2x + 3 < 17?
List the whole numbers with 3 < x <= 6.
